title: The burning house (Kern ch. 3)
hook: a father lures his children from a burning house with promises of carts, then gives them the finest cart

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekayana: the three vehicles were skillful means, and underneath them is one vehicle, to Buddhahood. Your line: one vehicle. Did you spot one want under two different ways? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

Smoke is already coming through the roof. The house is old, the beams are rotten, and there is only one door. Out in the yard stands the owner, a rich old man. Inside, his children are playing, so absorbed in their games that they haven't noticed a thing. He shouts fire. They look up, puzzled, and go back to playing. They don't know what fire is, or what a house on fire means. This is the parable at the heart of chapter three, told by the Buddha to Sariputra. Today: the burning house.
screen: `SMOKE THROUGH THE ROOF.` → `ONE DOOR, CHILDREN PLAYING.` → `HE SHOUTS FIRE. NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, the father's problem. In Kern's telling, he thinks of gathering the children in his strong arms and carrying them out. But the door is narrow, and they are running everywhere. Shouting the truth hasn't worked. So he tries something else. Second, the promise. He knows what each child loves. He calls out: the toys you've always wanted are outside the door, carts drawn by goats, carts drawn by deer, carts drawn by bullocks. Come and get them. Hearing that, the children rush out together, pushing past each other, and are safe in the open air. Third, the gift. Out in the yard they ask for their carts. The father gives each child the same thing, and it isn't any of the three. It's a great cart drawn by white bullocks, swift, high, decked with jewels and hung with bells, finer than anything they asked for. He is rich enough, the story says, and they are all equally his children, so why give any of them less? Fourth, the question. Now the Buddha turns to Sariputra: did that father tell a lie? No, Sariputra answers. He saved their lives. Even if he had given them nothing, he would not have lied, because getting them out was the point. The Buddha then explains the picture. The house is the world, burning with suffering. The children are beings, absorbed in play. The three carts are the three vehicles from yesterday. The great cart is the one vehicle. And the father is the Buddha, who uses skillful means because shouting the plain truth reaches no one who doesn't yet know what fire is. Remember the question from two days ago, whether shaping the message is honest. Here is the sutra's own answer, in a story: a promise made out of love, and kept more generously than anyone asked.
screen: `THE DOOR IS NARROW.` · `GOAT, DEER AND BULLOCK CARTS.` · `ONE GREAT CART FOR EACH CHILD.` · `WAS THE FATHER A LIAR?` · then, large: `OUT OF THE BURNING HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: help someone out of danger kindly. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Think of someone you care about who is stuck in something that isn't good for them, small or large: overwork, a bad habit, a room they won't leave. Notice the urge to shout fire at them. Set it down for a moment. Then ask: what does this person love? What would make them want to walk toward the door on their own? Let one gentle idea come, if one comes. Keep it. The bell holds the time.
The burning house. The Lotus Sutra's parable of a father who calls his children out of a fire with the promise of carts, then gives each of them the finest cart of all. Today's word.
Your line: out of the burning house. Today, if you need to warn someone about something, start from what they love, not from the smoke. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: The parable of the burning house from chapter three of the Lotus Sutra has been retold in sermons, art and study in East Asian Buddhism, as the sutra's picture of skillful means and the one vehicle.

original.note: Sanskrit: comparison, parable; the name of chapter three, where the burning house is told.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a fire and some lucky kids.
what it means: the Buddha, like the father, uses skillful means to draw beings out of suffering, then gives them all the one vehicle.
what a scholar hears: the parable answers the honesty question about upaya; Sariputra's verdict, that the father told no lie, is the chapter's defense of skillful means.

notes: Chapter 3 parable paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted. Check: one door, the father's thought of carrying the children, the three carts (goat, deer, bullock), the single great cart drawn by white bullocks, and Sariputra's answer that it was no lie.
Kern's text gives the number of children and other figures; omitted under the claims rule.
In the sutra Sariputra's prediction comes before the parable; the index puts the parable first (day 1154) and the promise second (day 1155). Scripts follow the index.
